claim: P-TEFb is a critical coactivator for transcription of most cellular and viral genes, including those of HIV.
source: The positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) is a critical coactivator for transcription of most cellular and viral genes, including those of HIV.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about P-TEFb function.

claim: P-TEFb is regulated by 7SK snRNA in proliferating cells.
source: While P-TEFb is regulated by 7SK snRNA in proliferating cells, P-TEFb is absent due to diminished levels of CycT1 in quiescent and terminally differentiated cells, which has remained unexplored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about P-TEFb regulation.

claim: P-TEFb is absent due to diminished levels of CycT1 in quiescent and terminally differentiated cells.
source: While P-TEFb is regulated by 7SK snRNA in proliferating cells, P-TEFb is absent due to diminished levels of CycT1 in quiescent and terminally differentiated cells, which has remained unexplored.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation that motivates the study.

claim: CycT1 not bound to CDK9 is rapidly degraded in quiescent and terminally differentiated cells.
source: In these cells, we found that CycT1 not bound to CDK9 is rapidly degraded.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Productive CycT1:CDK9 interactions are increased by PKC-mediated phosphorylation of CycT1 in human cells.
source: Moreover, productive CycT1:CDK9 interactions are increased by PKC-mediated phosphorylation of CycT1 in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Dephosphorylation of CycT1 by PP1 reverses the process of P-TEFb assembly.
source: Conversely, dephosphorylation of CycT1 by PP1 reverses this process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with phosphatase inhibitors.

claim: PKC inhibitors result in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation.
source: Thus, PKC inhibitors or removal of PKC by chronic activation results in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with PKC inhibitors.

claim: Removal of PKC by chronic activation results in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation.
source: Thus, PKC inhibitors or removal of PKC by chronic activation results in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PMA treatment experiments.

claim: P-TEFb depletion occurs in resting CD4+ T cells.
source: This finding not only recapitulates P-TEFb depletion in resting CD4+ T cells but also in anergic T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding that connects the mechanism to biological contexts.

claim: P-TEFb depletion occurs in anergic T cells.
source: This finding not only recapitulates P-TEFb depletion in resting CD4+ T cells but also in anergic T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with W131AOTII mice.

claim: Clearance of RNAPII from promoters requires the phosphorylation of its C-terminal domain (CTD) at position 5 (Ser5) by CDK7 from TFIIH.
source: Clearance of RNAPII from promoters requires the phosphorylation of its C-terminal domain (CTD) at position 5 (Ser5) in tandemly repeated heptapeptide (52 repeats of Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7) by cyclin-dependent kinase 7 (CDK7) from the transcription factor-II H (TFIIH) (Chapman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Promoters of most inactive and inducible genes are already engaged by stalled RNAPII.
source: Of interest, promoters of most inactive and inducible genes are already engaged by stalled RNAPII, which departs from the transcription start site (TSS) but pauses after transcribing 20–100-nucleotides-long transcripts (Rahl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The pause of RNAPII is caused by NELF and DSIF.
source: The pause of RNAPII is caused by two factors, the negative elongation factor (NELF) (Yamaguchi et al., 1999) and DRB sensitivity-inducing factor (DSIF) (Wada et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The release of RNAPII for productive elongation requires P-TEFb.
source: The release of RNAPII for productive elongation requires the positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), which is composed of cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) and C-type cyclins T1 or T2 (CycT1 or CycT2) (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: P-TEFb is composed of CDK9 and CycT1 or CycT2.
source: The release of RNAPII for productive elongation requires the positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), which is composed of cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) and C-type cyclins T1 or T2 (CycT1 or CycT2) (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: CycT1 is expressed ubiquitously compared to the largely restricted expression of CycT2.
source: Compared to the largely restricted expression of CycT2, CycT1 is expressed ubiquitously (Peng et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: CDK9 phosphorylates Spt5 in DSIF and NELF-E, which relieve the pausing of RNAPII.
source: CDK9 is a Ser/Thr proline-directed kinase (i.e., PITALRE) (Graña et al., 1994) that phosphorylates Spt5 in DSIF and NELF-E, which relieve the pausing of RNAPII (Fujinaga et al., 2004; Ivanov et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: After phosphorylation by CDK9, NELF is released and DSIF is converted to an elongation factor.
source: After phosphorylation, NELF is released and DSIF is converted to an elongation factor (Wada et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Serine at position 2 (Ser2) in the CTD is phosphorylated by CDK9 before RNAPII's transition to productive elongation.
source: Serine at position 2 (Ser2) in the CTD is also phosphorylated by CDK9 before RNAPII's transition to productive elongation (Peterlin and Price, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: 7SK snRNP sequesters 50 to 90% of P-TEFb in different cells in an inactive state.
source: To ensure this balance, a large complex, known as the 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (7SK snRNP), sequesters a large amount of P-TEFb (from 50 to 90% in different cells) in an inactive state (Peterlin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: 7SK snRNP consists of 7SK snRNA, HEXIM1/2 proteins, LARP7, and MePCE.
source: 7SK snRNP consists of the abundant 7SK small nuclear RNA (7SK snRNA), hexamethylene bisacetamide (HMBA)-inducible mRNAs 1 and 2 (HEXIM1/2) proteins, La-related protein 7 (LARP7), and methyl phosphate capping enzyme (MePCE) (Michels and Bensaude, 2008; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Dysregulation of the P-TEFb equilibrium contributes to various diseases such as solid tumors, leukemias and lymphomas, and cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Dysregulation of the P-TEFb equilibrium contributes to various diseases such as solid tumors (mutation in LARP7), leukemias and lymphomas (DNA translocations leading to aberrant recruitment of P-TEFb), and cardiac hypertrophy (inactivation of HEXIM1) (Franco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Cellular stresses such as UV irradiation and heat promote the release of P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP in a reversible manner.
source: Cellular stresses such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation and heat, as well as various small compounds such as histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), HMBA and bromodomain extra-terminal domain (BET) inhibitors (JQ1), also promote the release of P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP in a reversible manner (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Various small compounds such as HDACi, HMBA and BET inhibitors promote the release of P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP in a reversible manner.
source: Cellular stresses such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation and heat, as well as various small compounds such as histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), HMBA and bromodomain extra-terminal domain (BET) inhibitors (JQ1), also promote the release of P-TEFb from the 7SK snRNP in a reversible manner (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Different viruses such as HIV, HTLV, EBV, HSV, HCMV have evolved different strategies to utilize P-TEFb for their own replication.
source: Despite these important cellular responses, different viruses, such as HIV, HTLV, EBV, HSV, HCMV, and others, have evolved different strategies to utilize P-TEFb for their own replication (Mbonye et al., 2013; Zaborowska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: HIV Tat binds to free P-TEFb and promotes the release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP.
source: For example, the HIV transactivator of transcription (Tat) not only binds to free P-TEFb but also promotes the release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an example of viral strategy.

claim: Tat:P-TEFb binds to the TAR RNA stem loop to activate the transcription of viral genes.
source: Tat:P-TEFb then binds to the trans-activation response (TAR) RNA stem loop to activate the transcription of viral genes (Selby and Peterlin, 1990; Wei et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The establishment of viral latency in quiescent cells parallels the disappearance of P-TEFb.
source: Additionally, the establishment of viral latency in quiescent cells parallels the disappearance of P-TEFb, which can be reversed by cell activation (Rice, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: High levels of P-TEFb are found in activated and proliferating cells.
source: In activated and proliferating cells, high levels of P-TEFb are found.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: P-TEFb levels are vanishingly low in resting cells, especially monocytes and memory T cells.
source: In contrast, they are vanishingly low in resting cells, especially monocytes and memory T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: While levels of CDK9 persist, those of CycT1 are greatly reduced in resting cells.
source: While levels of CDK9 persist, those of CycT1 are greatly reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Transcripts for CycT1 and CDK9 remain high in resting and activated cells.
source: At the same time, transcripts for CycT1 and CDK9 remain high in all these cells (Garriga et al., 1998; Ghose et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: CDK9 is stabilized by chaperone proteins HSP70 and HSP90 in quiescent cells.
source: In these cells, CDK9 is stabilized by chaperone proteins HSP70 and HSP90 (O'Keeffe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: It was previously thought that CycT1 translation is inhibited by RNAi in quiescent cells.
source: For CycT1, it was thought that its translation is inhibited by RNAi (Chiang and Rice, 2012; Sung and Rice, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations as a previous hypothesis.

claim: CycT1 is rapidly degraded in quiescent cells.
source: In contrast, we find that CycT1 is rapidly degraded in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the current study.

claim: The unbound CycT1 protein can be stabilized by proteasomal inhibitors.
source: Importantly, the unbound CycT1 protein can be stabilized by proteasomal inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the current study.

claim: Residues in the N-terminal region of CycT1 (positions 1–280) are required for interactions between CycT1 and CDK9.
source: Previously, residues in the N-terminal region of CycT1 (positions 1–280, CycT1(280), including cyclin boxes, positions 30–248) (Figure 1A) were found to be required for interactions between CycT1 and CDK9 (Garber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A substitution of leucine to proline at position 203 (L203P) in CycT1 completely abolished binding to CDK9.
source: In particular, a substitution of the leucine to proline at position 203 (L203P) or four substitutions from a glutamic to aspartic acid at position 137 and threonine to alanine at positions 143, 149, and 155 (4MUT) completely abolished this binding (Kuzmina et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Four substitutions (E137D, T143A, T149A, T155A) in CycT1 completely abolished binding to CDK9.
source: In particular, a substitution of the leucine to proline at position 203 (L203P) or four substitutions from a glutamic to aspartic acid at position 137 and threonine to alanine at positions 143, 149, and 155 (4MUT) completely abolished this binding (Kuzmina et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P, CycT14MUT, and CycT1T3A) are poorly expressed in 293T cells.
source: Mutant CycT1 proteins were poorly expressed in 293T cells (Figure 1B, panel 1, lanes 3, 5, and 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression levels of mutant CycT1 proteins are restored by incubating cells with bortezomib.
source: Expression levels of these proteins were restored by incubating cells with the potent and clinically approved proteasomal inhibitor bortezomib (Figure 1B, panel 1, compare lanes 4, 6, and 8 to lanes 3, 5, and 7), indicating that these mutant CycT1 proteins are highly unstable in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutant CycT1 proteins are highly unstable in cells.
source: Expression levels of these proteins were restored by incubating cells with the potent and clinically approved proteasomal inhibitor bortezomib (Figure 1B, panel 1, compare lanes 4, 6, and 8 to lanes 3, 5, and 7), indicating that these mutant CycT1 proteins are highly unstable in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: The half-life of CycT1L203P is approximately 3 hours.
source: Whereas levels of the wild-type (WT) CycT1 protein remained unchanged after CHX treatment (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 1–4), those of three mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P, CycT14MUT, and CycT1T3A) decreased rapidly with the half-life of ~3 hr, ~ 2.5 hr, and ~6 hr, respectively (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 5–8; lanes 9–12; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 1C.

claim: The half-life of CycT14MUT is approximately 2.5 hours.
source: Whereas levels of the wild-type (WT) CycT1 protein remained unchanged after CHX treatment (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 1–4), those of three mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P, CycT14MUT, and CycT1T3A) decreased rapidly with the half-life of ~3 hr, ~ 2.5 hr, and ~6 hr, respectively (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 5–8; lanes 9–12; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 1C.

claim: The half-life of CycT1T3A is approximately 6 hours.
source: Whereas levels of the wild-type (WT) CycT1 protein remained unchanged after CHX treatment (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 1–4), those of three mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P, CycT14MUT, and CycT1T3A) decreased rapidly with the half-life of ~3 hr, ~ 2.5 hr, and ~6 hr, respectively (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 5–8; lanes 9–12; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 1C.

claim: Levels of wild-type CycT1 protein remain unchanged after cycloheximide treatment.
source: Whereas levels of the wild-type (WT) CycT1 protein remained unchanged after CHX treatment (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 1–4), those of three mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P, CycT14MUT, and CycT1T3A) decreased rapidly with the half-life of ~3 hr, ~ 2.5 hr, and ~6 hr, respectively (Figure 1C, panel 1, lanes 5–8; lanes 9–12; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 1C.

claim: Levels of endogenous CDK9 protein are not changed under bortezomib treatment.
source: Moreover, levels of the endogenous CDK9 protein were not changed under bortezomib (Figure 1B, panel 2) or CHX treatment (data not provided).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutant CycT1L203P and CycT14MUT proteins do not interact with CDK9 when protein levels are restored by bortezomib.
source: When protein levels were restored by bortezomib, mutant CycT1 proteins (CycT1L203P and CycT14MUT) did not interact with CDK9 (Figure 1D, panel 1, compare lanes 4 and 5 to lane 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1D.

claim: Interactions between mutant CycT1T3A and CDK9 proteins are significantly decreased compared to wild-type.
source: Similarly, interactions between mutant CycT1T3A and CDK9 proteins were significantly decreased (Figure 1D, panel 1, compare lane 6 to lane 3, ~7.8-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1D.

claim: Mutant CycT1T143A protein exhibits significantly impaired binding to CDK9.
source: As presented in Figure 1E, whereas mutant CycT1T143A and CycT1T149A proteins exhibited significantly impaired binding to CDK9, the mutant CycT1T155A protein did not (panel 1, compare lanes 4 and 5 to lanes 2 and 6, ~5.2-fold and ~3.7-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutant CycT1T149A protein exhibits significantly impaired binding to CDK9.
source: As presented in Figure 1E, whereas mutant CycT1T143A and CycT1T149A proteins exhibited significantly impaired binding to CDK9, the mutant CycT1T155A protein did not (panel 1, compare lanes 4 and 5 to lanes 2 and 6, ~5.2-fold and ~3.7-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutant CycT1T155A protein does not exhibit impaired binding to CDK9.
source: As presented in Figure 1E, whereas mutant CycT1T143A and CycT1T149A proteins exhibited significantly impaired binding to CDK9, the mutant CycT1T155A protein did not (panel 1, compare lanes 4 and 5 to lanes 2 and 6, ~5.2-fold and ~3.7-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1E.

claim: Thr143 and Thr149, but not Thr155, are critical residues in CycT1 for binding to CDK9.
source: These results indicate that Thr143 and Thr149, but not Thr155, are critical residues in CycT1 for binding to CDK9.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Mutant CycT1(280)TT143149AA protein demonstrates reduced binding to CDK9 to a similar extent as the mutant CycT1(280)T3A protein.
source: Finally, the mutant CycT1(280) protein with double threonine substitution to alanine (CycT1(280)TT143149AA) demonstrated reduced binding to CDK9 to a similar extent as the mutant CycT1(280)T3A protein (Figure 1F, panel 1, compare lanes 4 and 5 to lane 2, ~7.2-fold and ~8.1-fold reduction).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 1F.

claim: Two threonine residues (Thr143 and Thr149) in CycT1 are critical for its binding to CDK9 to form P-TEFb.
source: Taken together, we conclude that two threonine residues (Thr143 and Thr149) in CycT1 are critical for its binding to CDK9 to form P-TEFb, and that mutant CycT1 proteins that do not interact or poorly interact with CDK9 are rapidly degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Mutant CycT1 proteins that do not interact or poorly interact with CDK9 are rapidly degraded by the proteasome.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments.

source: Phospho-threonine signals were increased in CycT1 and CycT1(280) proteins in the presence of high concentrations (1 μM) of okadaic acid and 150 nM calyculin A, which inhibit serine/threonine protein phosphatases (PP) 1 and 2A (Figure 2A and B, panel 3, lanes 4 and 5), but not by a low concentration (5 nM) of okadaic acid (Figure 2A and B, panel 3, lane 3), which only inhibits PP2A.

claim: The predominant contribution to the increased binding energy of the P-TEFb complex comes from electrostatic and polar solvation energies.

claim: Phosphates on Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 are essential for the assembly and stability of P-TEFb.

claim: Staurosporine exhibited the most significant inhibition of CycT1 in 293T cells among PKC inhibitors tested.

claim: Interactions between CycT1(280) and CDK9 are decreased by staurosporine, bisindolylmaleimide IX, and HBDDE.

claim: PKC inhibitors inhibit the phosphorylation of CycT1 and its interactions with CDK9, which results in the degradation of CycT1 in 293T cells.
source: Thus, PKC inhibitors, especially staurosporine, inhibit the phosphorylation of CycT1 and its interactions with CDK9, which results in the degradation of CycT1 in 293T cells.

claim: Levels of endogenous CycT1 protein in Jurkat cells are significantly decreased by staurosporine in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: Levels of CDK9 are largely unaffected by staurosporine in Jurkat cells.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Bisindolylmaleimide IX decreases levels of the endogenous CycT1 protein in Jurkat cells in a dose-dependent manner.

As presented in Figure 4E, levels of CycT1 were decreased by bisindolylmaleimide IX ~4-fold at 6 μM and ~10-fold at 12 μM (panel 1, compare lanes 3 and 4 to lane 1).

claim: H-7 decreases levels of the endogenous CycT1 protein in Jurkat cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Similar to staurosporine, two additional PKC inhibitors, bisindolylmaleimide IX (Figure 4E) and H-7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), also decreased levels of the endogenous CycT1 protein in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bisindolylmaleimide IX decreases CycT1 up to 20-fold at 3, 6, and 12 μM in activated primary CD4+ T cells from donor 1.

source: As presented in Figure 6F, CycT1 expression in activated primary T cells from a donor began to decrease at 24 hr (panel 1, compare lane 2 to lane 1, ~1.8-fold reduction) after the addition of ionomycin (1 μM) and continued at 48 hr (panel 1, compare lane 3 to lane 1, ~4.5-fold reduction) and 72 hr (panel 1, compare lane 4 to lane 1, ~9.1-fold reduction).

claim: Levels of CDK9 are largely unaffected by ionomycin treatment in activated primary CD4+ T cells.
source: Levels of CDK9 were largely unaffected (Figure 6F, panel 2, lanes 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 6F.

claim: The absence of active PKC correlates with significant decreases of CycT1, which prevents the assembly of the functional P-TEFb complex.
source: Taken together, the absence of active PKC correlates with significant decreases of CycT1, which prevents the assembly of the functional P-TEFb complex.

claim: Mutations of two critical residues in CycT1 (Thr143 and Thr149 to alanine) impair its binding to CDK9.
source: In this study, we found that mutations of two critical residues in CycT1 (Thr143 and Thr149 to alanine) impair its binding to CDK9.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 promotes CycT1:CDK9 interactions.
source: Phosphorylation of these residues promotes CycT1:CDK9 interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Structural modeling indicated that phosphates on Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 increase intramolecular and intermolecular binding to specific residues in CycT1 and CDK9.
source: Structural modeling indicated that phosphates on Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 increase intramolecular and intermolecular binding to specific residues in CycT1 and CDK9, respectively, which contributes to P-TEFb assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: PKC inhibitors inhibit CycT1 phosphorylation.
source: Indeed, PKC inhibitors inhibited CycT1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: PKCα and PKCβ bind to CycT1 and promote CycT1:CDK9 interactions and stabilize CycT1 in vivo and in vitro.
source: Of PKC isoforms, PKCα and PKCβ were found not only to bind to CycT1 but to promote CycT1:CDK9 interactions and stabilize CycT1 in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Depleting PKC or its inactivity leads to CycT1 dissociation from CDK9 and its degradation in transformed cell lines as well as primary activated and anergic T cells.
source: Finally, depleting PKC or its inactivity led to CycT1 dissociation from CDK9 and its degradation in transformed cell lines as well as primary activated and anergic T cells.

source: We conclude that the assembly and stability of P-TEFb are potentiated by the phosphorylation of CycT1, which is regulated by PKCα, PKCβ, and PP1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Thr143, 149, and 155 in CycT1 are conserved in over 142 mammalian species and in CycT2.
source: They are conserved in over 142 mammalian species and in CycT2 (sequences are picked out from NCBI and aligned).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on sequence analysis.

claim: Previous reports indicated that Thr143, 149, and 155 play critical roles in P-TEFb function.
source: Moreover, previous reports indicated that these residues play critical roles in P-TEFb function (Jadlowsky et al., 2008; Kuzmina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 is blocked by a high dose of okadaic acid, which inhibits PP1 and PP2A.
source: Dephosphorylation of these residues was blocked by a high dose of okadaic acid, which inhibits PP1 and PP2A, or the general PP inhibitor calyculin A, but not by a low dose of okadaic acid, which inhibits only PP2A (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: PP1, and not PP2A, is the candidate for CycT1 dephosphorylation.
source: These results indicate that PP1, and not PP2A, is the candidate for CycT1 dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the experimental results.

claim: PP1 contains 3 catalytic and over 50 regulatory subunits, whose genetic inactivation is lethal to cells.
source: PP1 contains 3 catalytic and over 50 regulatory subunits, whose genetic inactivation is lethal to cells (Cohen, 2002; Ferreira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: PP1 regulates cell cycle cyclins, such as CycB, CycD1, and AIB1.
source: Indeed, they are phosphatases that regulate cell cycle cyclins, such as CycB, CycD1, and AIB1 (Edelson and Brautigan, 2011; Ferrero et al., 2011; Vorlaufer and Peters, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: PKCα and PKCβ isoforms phosphorylate Thr143 and Thr149 in CycT1 in vitro.
source: As to kinases, PKCα and PKCβ isoforms phosphorylate these two threonine residues in CycT1 in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The depletion of PKC results in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation, which explains cells becoming unresponsive to external stimuli.
source: Importantly, our study also reveals that the depletion of PKC, as occurs after chronic activation or phorbol ester treatment, results in P-TEFb disassembly and CycT1 degradation, which explains cells becoming unresponsive to external stimuli.

claim: Tat no longer functions in cells treated with phorbol esters because of P-TEFb depletion.
source: It also explains why Tat, whose coactivator is P-TEFb, no longer functions in such cells (Jakobovits et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for a previous observation, with a citation.

claim: Anergic cells lack P-TEFb, which contributes to their unresponsive phenotype.
source: Anergic cells also lack P-TEFb (Figure 6D), which contributes to their unresponsive phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Resting and memory T cells lack P-TEFb.
source: From our and other studies, we also know that resting and memory T cells lack P-TEFb (Garriga et al., 1998; Ghose et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Proviral latency is maintained in resting and memory T cells due to lack of P-TEFb.
source: Thus, proviral latency is maintained in these cells (Fujinaga and Cary, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

source: This situation most likely pertains to other DNA viruses, such as HSV and HTLV1/2, in yet other resting or terminally differentiated cells (Kulkarni and Bangham, 2018; Nicoll et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation with citations to support the claim.

source: For example, CycE unbound to its kinase partner CDK2 is rapidly degraded via SCF E3 ligase-mediated proteasomal pathway (Clurman et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The transcriptional cyclins/CDKs display and mimic regulatory paradigms of cell cycle cyclins/CDKs.
source: Thus, the transcriptional cyclins/CDKs display and mimic regulatory paradigms of cell cycle cyclins/CDKs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the comparison.

claim: The regulation of P-TEFb by phosphorylation is very different from the P-TEFb equilibrium in growing, proliferating cells, where 7SK snRNP plays the major role.
source: This regulation is also very different from the P-TEFb equilibrium in growing, proliferating cells, where 7SK snRNP plays the major role.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a comparison of regulatory mechanisms.

source: In this RNP, HEXIM1 or HEXIM2 inhibit CDK9 by binding to its ATP pocket, a situation that is reminiscent of CDK2 inhibition by p21 (Russo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Levels of CycT1 and CDK9 mRNAs do not vary between resting and activated T cells.
source: However, levels of CycT1 and CDK9 mRNAs do not vary between resting and activated T cells (Marshall et al., 2005), between responsive and anergic T cells or exhausted T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Global mRNA sequencing studies underestimate contributions of P-TEFb and/or other transcriptional CDKs in their evaluations of target genes.
source: This finding is important as these global studies do not look at levels of resulting proteins. Thus, they underestimate contributions of P-TEFb and/or other transcriptional CDKs in their evaluations of target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a critique of global studies.

claim: P-TEFb must be recruited by transcription factors to the paused RNAPII at promoter-proximal regions.
source: Additionally, P-TEFb must be recruited by transcription factors to the paused RNAPII at promoter-proximal regions.

claim: P-TEFb can mediate short and long distance interactions between enhancers and promoters to promote transcription elongation and co-transcriptional processing of individual and clusters of genes.
source: Indeed, P-TEFb can mediate short and long distance interactions between enhancers and promoters to promote transcription elongation and co-transcriptional processing of individual and clusters of genes (Taube et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The C-terminal His-rich region of CycT1 interacts directly with the CTD of RNAPII.
source: In this scenario, the C-terminal His-rich region of CycT1 interacts directly with the CTD of RNAPII (Taube et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Post-translational modifications of P-TEFb play critical roles in activated transcription and for growth and proliferation of cells.
source: Thus, these post-translational modifications of P-TEFb play critical roles in activated transcription and for growth and proliferation of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: In quiescent cells, only basal transcription is detected.
source: In quiescent cells, only basal transcription is detected (Cheung and Rando, 2013; Roche et al., 2017).

source: Importantly, external stimuli can reverse this phenotype via this reversible phosphorylation of P-TEFb.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study.

source: As a result, effects of potent activators, such as cMyc, NF-κB, steroid hormones, CIITA, etc., are translated to the productive transcription of their target genes (Fujinaga, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Targeted phosphatase inhibitors might prevent the establishment of proviral latency.

source: To this end, bortezomib and other proteasomal inhibitors have been examined already for the reversal of HIV latency in resting CD4+ T cells (Cary and Peterlin, 2020; Li et al., 2019).
